title: Dedicated capacity buyers brief: SLA, throughput, isolation
content:
Executive summary:

This briefing is a procurement-ready sales play for Redwood’s Dedicated offering focused on the three buyer pillars: SLA guarantees, tenant isolation (data and tenancy), and predictable throughput / capacity economics. The doc is written for AE/solutions engineers preparing commercial proposals and for procurement teams evaluating enterprise inference vendors. It includes TL;DR talking points, an RFP-compatible SLA appendix, a compact competitor comparison narrative, and negotiation levers that preserve price while addressing customer risk.

Why this matters to buyers:
- Predictability: Enterprise LLM workloads require steady throughput for user-facing features (chat, embeddings, reranking). Unpredictable costs or throttles cause customer-facing outages and chaos in product roadmaps.
- Isolation & compliance: Regulated customers need clear boundaries around model execution, logging, and key management. Shared noisy neighbors are a blockers for procurement.
- Accountability: Procurement demands measurable, enforceable SLAs with clear remediation (service credits, fallback policies) rather than vague promises.

Key value propositions for procurement conversations:
1) Deterministic throughput slices: Redwood Dedicated reserves GPU capacity with hard reservations expressed as "tokens-per-minute" or "concurrent-generation units". Customers can map these to production QPS or peak-hour needs and receive predictable latency distributions (p50/p90/p99 profiles) in the contract.
2) Measured SLOs and service credits: Offer a contract clause with uptime targets (example: 99.95% availability per calendar month for control plane and 99.9% for GPU inference endpoints) and clear credit formulas. Emphasize observability: per-route latency histograms, token-level cost breakdown, and exportable traces for audits.
3) Tenant isolation options: Provide two isolation tiers — logical isolation (dedicated model-serving pools, shared infra but isolated tenancy) and physical isolation (single-tenant nodes or VPC-on-prem bundles). Call out KMS/HSM integrations and audit log retention windows (configurable).
4) Graceful degradation: Built-in fallbacks: when primary capacity is constrained, traffic is routed to pinned compatible model variants or burst pools. This gives product teams graceful quality/latency trade-offs instead of hard failures.

Procurement-ready messaging snippets (short):
- "We sell reserved inference capacity — predictable bills, predictable latency, and verifiable SLAs backed by service credits and playbooks."
- "Choose logical isolation for strong multi-tenant protections; choose physical isolation when regulatory or auditing requirements demand hardware-level separation and customer-managed networking."
- "You get per-route SLO dashboards and daily exportable logs to satisfy auditors and reduce MTTI for incidents."

Suggested RFP language (copy-paste friendly):
- Capacity: Vendor shall reserve and guarantee the equivalent of X concurrent inference units supporting Y tokens/sec sustained with documented p50/p90/p99 latency for text generation at Z context length.
- Availability: Vendor shall provide 99.9% availability for the inference endpoints and 99.95% for the control plane measured monthly. Service credits shall apply on a sliding scale starting at 99.85% availability.
- Isolation & Data Handling: Vendor shall provide tenant isolation options (logical and physical) and must support customer-managed encryption keys (KMS/HSM) and configurable audit log retention of at least 365 days.
- Response to incidents: Vendor shall provide 24x7 incident response for P1 outages with an initial acknowledgement within 15 minutes and regular updates until mitigation.

Compact competitor narrative (for quick AE prep):
- Hyperscaler managed endpoints: Strengths include low friction and large data center footprint. Weaknesses are opaque noisy-neighbor behavior, limited per-tenant isolation, and less predictable per-token economics.
- Boutique inference vendors: Often offer strong isolation and customized SLAs, but they typically lack a large model catalog, have higher per-token cost, and limited tooling for route-level observability.
- Open-source self-hosted setups: Lowest vendor lock-in but high operational burden; engineering teams must build batching, fallback, and cost controls.

How Redwood wins:
- Balanced offering across the stack: dedicated reservations, VPC/private deployment options, and a runtime designed for high-throughput inference with built-in batching and KV caching.
- Observable contracts: We provide per-route telemetry by default and a standardized service credit schedule that reduces procurement friction.
- Flexible isolation: Logical isolation for cost-sensitive customers; physical isolation for regulated industries.

Negotiation levers and what to concede vs. hold:
- Concede (low risk): Longer SLA measurement windows (monthly vs. hourly), slightly higher availability targets on control plane vs. inference endpoints, extended onboarding timelines, additional export formats for logs.
- Hold (high value): Guaranteed throughput units without hidden throttles, core latency p99 targets, customer-managed KMS/HSM and audit retention, indemnities around data handling.
- Tradeable items: Onboarding credits, fixed-price transition periods, professional services days for integration, committed burst budget for seasonal traffic.

Sample Service Credit schedule (example):
- >= 99.90% uptime: no credit
- 99.80% - 99.90%: 10% monthly service credit on invoice for impacted endpoints
- 99.00% - 99.79%: 25% monthly service credit
- < 99.00%: 50% monthly service credit plus negotiated remediation plan

Sales play & checklist for proposal creation:
1) Run quick sizing call with customer engineering to translate QPS and prompt length into concurrent-generation units.
2) Propose a reserve + burst model: baseline reserved units for predictability, short-term burst credits for growth periods.
3) Pick isolation tier and list any additional compliance needs (SOC2, ISO, FedRAMP conversation).
4) Attach the SLA addendum and observable deliverables: dashboards, exportable logs, and runbook access.
5) Offer 30–90 day performance validation: trial with defined metrics and exit criteria.

Sample objection handling scripts (AE):
- "Your price is high vs. shared API." -> "Dedicated is priced for predictable TCO: fewer surprises, consistent latency and lower overall engineering ops cost required to self-manage. We can model three scenarios and show break-even weeks."
- "We need physical isolation only." -> "We support an on-prem / VPC private deployment with customer-managed KMS and optional hardware isolation; we’ll map architecture during the PO stage and include explicit audit controls in the SOW."

Appendix A — Example SLA clause (boilerplate start):
- "Service Level. Vendor will provide the Dedicated Inference Service with a Monthly Availability of at least 99.9% for inference endpoints. Monthly Availability is measured as (TotalMinutes - DowntimeMinutes)/TotalMinutes. Downtime excludes scheduled maintenance with 72-hour notice. If Monthly Availability is below the threshold, Customer will be eligible for Service Credits as set forth in the Service Credit schedule."

Appendix B — Observability deliverables (exportable):
- Per-route latency histograms (p50/p90/p99) over configurable retention windows
- Token-level cost reports by route and by model version
- Audit logs for model input/output metadata (configurable redact rules)
- Access to incident traces and SRE postmortem artifacts for P1 incidents

Appendix C — Example procurement Q&A (short):
- Q: How do you measure availability? A: We measure at the route/endpoint level from our load balancers to the inference pool and exclude scheduled maintenance.
- Q: What is the recommended reservation sizing buffer? A: Start at 1.3x observed peak QPS for the first quarter, then tune down with autoscaling policies and cache hit metrics.
- Q: Can we bring our own keys? A: Yes — KMS and HSM integrations supported for private and dedicated customers.

Next steps for the GTM team:
- Finalize a one-page SLA addendum that legal can fast-track for deals < $250k ARR.
- Create an AE-facing one-pager with the sizing calculator and competitor callouts.
- Package a 60-day trial playbook that includes telemetry collection, success criteria, and an executive ROI slide.

Notes / open questions:
- Need to align with finance on refundable vs. non-refundable reservation commitments for churn scenarios.
- Confirm standard audit log retention tiering and pricing for >365 days retention.
- Validate the final service credit language with legal (cap on total credits, exclusion of force majeure).

Owners for follow-ups: Marketing: Evelyn Cho (messaging), Solutions Eng: Marco Hernandez (sizing playbook), Legal & Finance liaison: Samir Gupta.

End of brief.
